They differ on whether the charge cuts plastic use. A says shoppers have 'taken 60% fewer plastic bags'. B says 'I use just as much plastic as before'. They are similar in showing that shoppers do pay the charge. A speaks of 'the money collected' and B says 'I now pay for bags'.

They differ on whether the charge cuts plastic use. A says shoppers have 'taken 60% fewer plastic bags'. B says 'I use just as much plastic as before'. They are similar in showing that shoppers do pay the charge. A speaks of 'the money collected' and B says 'I now pay for bags'. They also differ in purpose. A wants the public to see the charge as a success and the chain as responsible, so it gives a figure and mentions the fund. B wants neighbours to feel the charge only costs them money, so it points to the bill.
It is useful because it is from an environment group and it is about plastic bags.

It is useful. It shows the charge has cut the number of bags: 'Plastic bags are down by more than half'. It is limited. It counts only the bags taken at shops. It says nothing about other plastic that people buy instead.

It is useful. It shows the charge has cut the number of bags: 'Plastic bags are down by more than half'. It is limited. It counts only the bags taken at shops. Source B says she buys 'rolls of bin liners' and uses 'just as much plastic as before'. So C's figure covers bags at the till only. C is also a leaflet handed out while the charge was being reviewed, by a group that wants it extended 'to every shop and stall', so it shows only the good result. It is useful for bags taken at shops, not for plastic waste as a whole.
I agree because plastic is bad for the environment and people should bring their own bags.
I agree. Source A says shoppers have 'taken 60% fewer plastic bags', so less plastic is being given out. Source C also agrees: bags are 'down by more than half', so the charge is working.

I agree to some extent. Source A says shoppers have 'taken 60% fewer plastic bags', so less plastic is being given out. Source C also agrees: bags are 'down by more than half'. Source B disagrees. She uses 'just as much plastic as before' because she now buys bin liners. Source D partly disagrees too: there is 'more loose rubbish in the chutes', so the estate is dirtier.

Source A says shoppers have 'taken 60% fewer plastic bags', so less plastic is being given out. Source C also agrees: bags are 'down by more than half'. Source B disagrees. She uses 'just as much plastic as before' because she now buys bin liners. Source D partly disagrees too: there is 'more loose rubbish in the chutes'. The sources that agree are weaker. A comes from the supermarket and C from a group that wants the charge extended, and both count only bags at the till. B is one resident, but D sees many blocks and reports both a gain and a loss, so D is the most balanced. So I agree only to some extent: fewer bags are handed out, but part of the waste has moved elsewhere.
The workers sat at the field on Sundays and some residents called the police.
The residents were unwelcoming to the workers.

The residents saw the workers as a threat even when they did nothing wrong. They 'called the police though we were only eating'. Calling the police on people having a meal shows the residents were suspicious of the workers themselves, not of anything they did.
It is reliable because it is written by a resident who lives in the estate.
It is not reliable because it uses strong words like 'will not be safe' and it wants the dormitory built 'somewhere else'.

It is not reliable. A claims children 'will not be safe'. But Source C reports that in three estates with dormitories 'reported crime did not rise' in the two years after they opened. The record from other estates does not support A's fear.

It is not reliable. A claims children 'will not be safe'. But Source C reports that in three estates with dormitories 'reported crime did not rise' in the two years after they opened. The record from other estates does not support A's fear. A is also a letter to the MP, passed round the estate chat, by a resident who wants the dormitory built 'somewhere else'. It is written to make the MP and the neighbours oppose the plan, so it states fears as facts and gives no evidence.

The group wants residents to feel it is unfair to turn the workers away, so that they accept the dormitory and do not speak against it at the dialogue.
Both sources are about delivery riders. Source A is a blog and Source B is an interview.
They are similar in showing that riders decide when to work. A says riders 'choose their own hours'. B says 'I can pick my hours'.

They are similar in showing that riders decide when to work. A says riders 'choose their own hours'. B says 'I can pick my hours'. They differ on whether riders are really free. A says riders are 'their own bosses'. B says if he turns down orders 'the app gives me fewer the next day'.

They are similar in showing that riders decide when to work. A says riders 'choose their own hours'. B says 'I can pick my hours'. They differ on whether riders are really free. A says riders are 'their own bosses'. B says if he turns down orders 'the app gives me fewer the next day'. They also differ in purpose. A is written by the platform for people who might sign up, so it speaks only of flexibility to make riding look attractive. B wants readers to see the risk riders carry, so he tells of three weeks with no pay.
It is useful because it is written by the platform that the riders work for.
It is useful. It shows that riders value flexible hours: 'Eight in ten say flexibility is the main reason they ride with us'.

It is useful. It shows that riders value flexible hours: 'Eight in ten say flexibility is the main reason they ride with us'. It is limited. It tells us only why riders join. It says nothing about their pay, or what happens when a rider cannot work.

It is useful. It shows that riders value flexible hours: 'Eight in ten say flexibility is the main reason they ride with us'. It is limited. It tells us only why riders join. Source C found that 71% 'work more than 44 hours a week' and 58% 'have no savings to cover a month without work'. So the flexibility in A sits beside long hours and no safety net, which A leaves out. A is the platform's own blog, written to draw new riders, so it shows only the best side. It is useful for why riders sign up, not for what the work is like.
I agree because food delivery is very convenient and many people use it every day.

I agree. Source A says 'eight in ten' riders give flexibility as the main reason they ride, so riders get work that fits their lives. Source D agrees: orders through the app are 'now half my sales', so the platform kept his stall open.

Source A says 'eight in ten' riders give flexibility as the main reason they ride, so riders get work that fits their lives. Source D agrees: orders through the app are 'now half my sales', so the platform kept his stall open. Source B disagrees. He fell off his bike and 'earned nothing for three weeks', so riders are not protected. Source C also disagrees: '58% have no savings to cover a month without work'.

Source A says 'eight in ten' riders give flexibility as the main reason they ride, so riders get work that fits their lives. Source D agrees: orders through the app are 'now half my sales', so the platform kept his stall open. Source B disagrees. He fell off his bike and 'earned nothing for three weeks'. Source C also disagrees: '58% have no savings to cover a month without work'. The sources that disagree are stronger on riders. A comes from the platform, which gains from saying so. D can be trusted about his own stall but admits he does 'not know what the riders earn'. C asked 500 riders, and B's story fits its figures. So I agree to some extent: platforms are good for stalls, but the riders carry the risk.
The writer's mother has dementia and the nearest centre is 40 minutes away by bus.
There is not enough care for the elderly near the estate.

Care is too far away for a family to use while holding a job. The nearest centre is '40 minutes away by bus', and the writer 'gave up my job' to mind her mother. When care is that far, the burden falls on the family.
It is reliable because the residents wrote it and they know their own void deck best.
It is reliable because it explains that the void deck is where children play and where weddings and wakes are held, and the centre will take it away.

It is not fully reliable. A says the centre 'will take all of it'. But Source B states the centre 'will use one-third of the void deck' and 'the rest stays open'. A also says residents were 'told, not asked', but B records 'two briefing sessions in March'. B contradicts A on both points.

It is written to get neighbours to 'sign to say no', so it makes the loss sound total and leaves out the briefings.
